htmlTitle: Eight billion, one doubling at a time
metaDescription: World population from 10,000 BCE to 2023 on a globe you can turn: every doubling gets the same screen time, and every number says where it came from.
ogDescription: One doubling of humanity took 1,442 years; a later one took 37. Scroll 12,000 years on a globe, pick a country, see where each number comes from.
imageAlt: Eight horizontal bars, one for each doubling of the world population since 5000 BCE, shrinking from 1,652 years to 37, next to a globe of golden dots
title: Eight billion, one doubling at a time
ldDescription: An interactive history of world population from 10,000 BCE to 2023: a globe with one dot per million people or coloured by density, a pace where each doubling takes equal time, the range of independent historical estimates, and every country against the world.
ldDatasetName: World population by country, 10,000 BCE to 2023, with independent historical estimates
ldDatasetDescription: Population of 165 countries in today’s borders at 68 points in time from 10,000 BCE to 2023 (Our World in Data: HYDE 3.3, Gapminder v7, UN World Population Prospects 2024), and estimates of world population by nine other authors before 1950.

hero.h1: Eight billion, one doubling at a time
hero.shareTitle: Copy a link that reopens this exact setup
hero.sub: Between 560 BCE and 882 CE the number of people on Earth doubled once, and it took 1,442 years. Between 1948 and 1985 it doubled again in 37. Scroll to watch it happen, then take the controls: pick a view, a starting point and a country, and every number on the page tells you where it came from.
hero.meta: Data: HYDE (2023); Gapminder (2022); UN WPP (2024), with major processing by Our World in Data · other estimates: US Census Bureau compilation

scroll.h2: All of history in one scroll
scroll.p1: Keep scrolling and time moves with you. In the dots view every dot is a million people, dropped at random inside today’s borders of the country they lived in. In the density view each country is coloured by how many people share one square kilometre.
scroll.p2: Drag the globe sideways to turn it. The switch in its corner changes every map on this page. The year of each billion is read off the same series, so it can differ by a year from the dates the UN announced.
scroll.globeLabel: Globe behind the world population figure; it fills up as you scroll

play.p1: The same globe, now with a play button. Drag it to turn it and hover over a country to see its number. Three settings change what you notice: the view, where the story starts and the pace.
play.p2: The pace matters most. If every year gets the same time on screen, the globe stays nearly empty for nine tenths of the run and everything happens in the last seconds. If every doubling of the world’s population gets the same time, the distant past flies by, because it doubled slowly, and the last century slows down.
play.globeLabel: Globe of world population; drag to turn it
play.chartLabel: World population over time with the range of other estimates; hover to move the globe
play.note: Under the globe, the orange line is the series the globe plays. The shaded band runs from the lowest to the highest estimate published by nine other authors, and the coloured strip shows whose data each stretch is. Hover over the chart to move the globe to that moment.

country.p1: Choose a country and a period. The globe turns to it, and the panel shows its population, its share of the world and its rank among 165 countries at every moment. You can also click a country on the globe.
country.p2: Borders are today’s. “Italy in 500 BCE” means the people who lived on the land that is Italy now, whatever state they belonged to.
country.globeLabel: Globe turned to the chosen country; click another country to choose it

frames.p: The same data as still frames, for print and for comparing at a glance. They follow the view you picked above. Click a frame to open it full size, and use the arrow keys to step through the rest.
frames.mapLabel: Map of world population in the chosen year

weak.p1: Before 1950 every figure is a reconstruction. Most of the world had no census. Historians work back from tax records, farmland, the size of cities and how many people a hectare could feed. For the year 1 CE, published estimates run from about 170 to 400 million, and most of them fall between 170 and 330.
weak.p2: Before 1700 the series has one figure per century, and before 1 CE one per thousand years. Between them the page assumes steady growth, so plagues and wars shorter than the gap do not show. The Black Death does, because it left the world smaller in 1400 than it had been in 1300.
weak.p3: The dots say how many people lived in a country, not where inside it: Siberia gets as many dots per square kilometre as Moscow. The page covers the 165 countries whose series goes all the way back to 10,000 BCE; the countries left out add up to about 75 million people today.
weak.s1: Our World in Data, Population — the series on every globe and chart.
weak.s2: Kees Klein Goldewijk, HYDE 3.3, History Database of the Global Environment, Utrecht University, 2023 — up to 1800.
weak.s3: Gapminder, Population v7, 2022 — 1800 to 1949.
weak.s4: United Nations, World Population Prospects 2024 — from 1950.
weak.s5: US Census Bureau, Historical Estimates of World Population, and the same table on Wikipedia — the band of other estimates.
weak.s6: Country outlines: Natural Earth, 1:110 million, public domain. Licences: HYDE, Gapminder and Our World in Data CC BY 4.0; UN World Population Prospects CC BY 3.0 IGO.

tldr.sub: Between 560 BCE and 882 CE the number of people on Earth doubled once, and it took 1,442 years. Between 1948 and 1985 it doubled again in 37.
tldr.b1: One billion around 1805, two billion by 1926, eight billion in 2022.
tldr.b2: The Black Death: by 1400 the world had fewer people than in 1300.
tldr.b3: The fastest growth ever: more than 2% a year in the 1960s, and a new billion roughly every 12 years after that.
tldr.b4: Before 1950 every figure is a reconstruction. For the year 1 CE, published estimates run from about 170 to 400 million.
tldr.b5: Borders are today’s, and the dots are dropped at random inside them.
tldr.src: Data: Our World in Data, built from HYDE 3.3, Gapminder and UN World Population Prospects 2024; other estimates: US Census Bureau compilation.

js.between: Between two data points: {a} ({av}) and {b} ({bv}). The page fills the gap assuming steady growth.
js.spread: From {lo} to {hi}: the highest is {x} times the lowest. The orange mark is the figure on this page.
js.estOne: Only one other estimate for this year.
js.after1950: After 1950 the figures come from censuses and population registers. For the world as a whole, UN editions usually differ by no more than 1–2%; for single countries, by more.
js.noEst: No other estimate was published close to this moment.
js.hintLinear: Even years: every year gets the same time on screen. Honest, but the globe stays almost empty until the last seconds.
js.hintLog: Slower near today: the stretch from 7,000 to 700 years ago takes as long as the one from 700 to 70 years ago.
js.hintDoubling: Even doublings: every doubling of the world’s population gets the same time. The distant past flies by; the last century slows down.
js.lbDots: 1 dot = 1 million people, dropped at random inside today’s borders
js.lbDensity: Each country coloured by people per km², from 0.1 to 1,000, on a scale where each step is ten times the one before
caps: Farming spreads. About 19 million people live on the whole planet.
By 3200 BCE the first cities and the first writing appear in Mesopotamia and Egypt.
Around 1 CE: some 230 million people, fewer than live in Indonesia today.
About 320 million people by the year 1000. Growth is slow, and a bad harvest or an epidemic can undo a century of it.
The Black Death. By 1400 the world has fewer people than it had in 1300.
Growth returns, slowly: half a billion by 1500.
One billion, around 1805. It took all of human history to get here.
Two billion by 1926: the second billion took 121 years.
The fastest growth ever: more than 2% a year in the 1960s, and a new billion roughly every 12 years after that.
Growth is slowing, but from a very large base: 8 billion in 2022.
